title: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
summary: How a search engine turns documents into term-to-document postings, answers Boolean queries by merging sorted lists, and ranks results with TF-IDF and cosine similarity, plus how Lucene compresses and updates it.
outcomes: Explain why an inverted index stores only the 1s of the term-document matrix and what the dictionary and postings hold
Build an inverted index by sort-based indexing and compute df, tf and collection frequency by hand
Trace the two-pointer postings merge, order AND terms by df, and explain when skip pointers help
Compute TF-IDF and cosine scores for a small collection and explain why idf and length normalization change the ranking
Explain gap plus variable byte compression and why Lucene writes immutable segments

lessons.title: From grep to the inverted index

blocks.md:
Suppose you want every document that mentions both *deploy* and *rollback*. The simplest method is a linear scan: read every document, every time, and check for the words. This is what `grep` does, and for a modest collection it is all you need: Shakespeare's collected works are a bit under one million words.

It stops working when the collection holds billions of words, when you want operators like *within 5 words of*, and when you want the **best** matches first instead of every match. The fix is to do the work once, ahead of time: build an **index**.

We will use one tiny collection through the whole course. Six documents, already lowercased:

- **d1**: the cache keeps the hot keys in the cache
- **d2**: the deploy broke the cache
- **d3**: roll back the deploy
- **d4**: the hot path skips the cache
- **d5**: a cache miss after the deploy
- **d6**: the miss rate fell after the roll back

A **term** is an indexed unit, usually a normalized word. These six documents contain 38 tokens and 17 distinct terms.

The most direct index is a **term-document incidence matrix**: one row per term, one column per document, and a 1 where the term occurs. A **Boolean query** combines terms with AND, OR and NOT and returns the set of documents that satisfy it. With the matrix, each operator becomes a bitwise operation on rows.

blocks.title: Term-document incidence matrix for six docs

scenes.caption: Each row is a term, each column a document. A 1 means the term occurs in that document. This is 7 terms of the 17 in the vocabulary.
Query deploy AND roll AND NOT cache. Pull the three rows: deploy is 011010, roll is 001001, cache is 110110.
NOT flips the cache row to 001001. Now every operator is a bitwise AND across the rows.
011010 AND 001001 AND 001001 = 001000: only d3 (roll back the deploy) matches.

blocks.prompt: Scale it up. A collection has 1 million documents of about 1000 words each, and 500,000 distinct terms. How many cells does the incidence matrix have, and at most how many of them can be 1?
blocks.reveal: The matrix has $500{,}000 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 5 \times 10^{11}$ cells, half a trillion. But each document has only about 1000 words, so there are at most $10^9$ ones. At least **99.8%** of the cells are zero. Storing the zeros is pure waste, which is the whole motivation for the next idea.

blocks.md:
An **inverted index** stores only the 1s. It has two parts:

- The **dictionary** (vocabulary): every distinct term once, plus statistics such as the **document frequency** $\mathrm{df}_t$, the number of documents that contain term $t$.
- For each term, a **postings list**: the docIDs of the documents containing it, sorted in increasing order. Each entry is a **posting**.

It is called inverted because it maps term to documents, the reverse of reading a document to find its terms.

blocks.title: Dictionary and postings for three terms

scenes.caption: The dictionary holds each distinct term once, with its document frequency (df): how many documents contain it.
Each term points to its postings list: the sorted docIDs of the documents that contain it. Only the 1s of the matrix are stored.
A query looks up each term in the dictionary and reads only those postings lists. Documents that contain neither term are never touched.
Intersecting 1, 2, 4, 5 with 5, 6 gives d5, the only document with both terms.

blocks.md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 4 and 5 add on top of the same postings.

blocks.question: Using the six documents, which documents match the Boolean query hot AND NOT deploy?
options: d1 and d4
d4 only
d1, d2, d4 and d5
No documents
blocks.explain: hot has postings d1, d4. deploy has postings d2, d3, d5, so NOT deploy is d1, d4, d6. The intersection is d1 and d4. Neither of them mentions deploy.

blocks.question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
blocks.explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 3). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

lessons.title: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings

blocks.md:
Index construction has four steps ([Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, ch. 1](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/a-first-take-at-building-an-inverted-index-1.html)):

1. Collect the documents and give each a **docID**, a unique integer, usually assigned in order of arrival.
2. **Tokenize**: split text into tokens, for example `Friends, Romans, countrymen.` into `Friends`, `Romans`, `countrymen`.
3. **Normalize**: map tokens to terms, for example lowercase and stem to `friend`, `roman`, `countryman`.
4. **Index**: record, for each term, the documents it occurs in.

The core of step 4 is **sort-based indexing**. Emit one (term, docID) pair per token, sort the pairs by term and then docID, merge repeated pairs from the same document, and split the result into a dictionary and postings lists. The watch below runs this on d1 to d3.

blocks.title: Sort-based indexing of d1 to d3

scenes.caption: Step 1: emit one (term, docID) pair per token, in document order. d1 to d3 produce 18 pairs.
Step 2: sort the pairs by term, then by docID. Equal terms are now adjacent and their docIDs are in increasing order.
Step 3: drop repeated (term, docID) pairs (greyed), keeping the count as the term frequency. 14 postings remain for 10 terms.
Step 4: each run of one term becomes a dictionary entry; its docIDs become the postings list. cache gets postings 1, 2 (df 2); the gets 1, 2, 3 (df 3).

blocks.md:
A posting can carry more than a docID. Most engines also store the **term frequency** $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$ (how many times $t$ occurs in $d$), which ranking needs. A **positional index** also stores the token positions, which phrase queries such as `"roll back"` need.

The dictionary is usually kept in memory and the much larger postings on disk. In memory, variable-length arrays beat linked lists on space and on cache-friendly scanning when updates are rare.

blocks.title: Building a tiny inverted index in Python

scenes.caption: Three documents, already lowercased. Real systems also strip punctuation and may stem words.
Tokenize and emit (term, docID) pairs in document order.
Sort: the core indexing step. Pairs for one term are now contiguous.
Group by term. Repeats inside one document increase a count instead of adding a posting.
Document frequency is just the length of each postings list.

blocks.prompt: Over all six documents, what is the document frequency of *the*, and what is its **collection frequency** (total occurrences across all documents)?
blocks.reveal: *the* is in every document, so $\mathrm{df} = 6$. Its counts per document are 3, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, so its collection frequency is **11**. The two statistics differ whenever a term repeats inside documents. Ranking will use df, because it measures how many documents a term can tell apart.

blocks.md: Whatever normalization you apply at index time (lowercasing, stemming, stripping punctuation) you must apply identically to queries. If the index stores `cache` and the query parser passes `Cache` through unchanged, the dictionary lookup finds nothing.

Stop words such as *the* can be dropped at index time to save space, but then a phrase made only of stop words, like *to be or not to be*, cannot be found. Lesson 4 shows that idf gives such words near-zero weight anyway, which weakens the case for dropping them.

blocks.question: A team lowercases text when indexing but forgets to lowercase queries. A user searches for Deploy. What happens on our six documents?
options: It matches d2, d3 and d5 as expected
It matches every document, because the lookup falls back to a scan
It matches nothing, because the dictionary contains deploy but not Deploy
It matches only d3, the document that starts with roll
blocks.explain: The dictionary is an exact lookup structure. Index-time and query-time analysis must agree, or terms simply miss. Search libraries let you configure one analyzer and apply it on both sides for exactly this reason.

blocks.question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
blocks.explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

lessons.title: Answering AND queries by merging postings

blocks.md:
Take a larger collection where *server* occurs in documents 2, 5, 9, 14, 21, 30, 38, 47 and *crash* in 5, 21, 40, 47. To answer `server AND crash`, look up both terms in the dictionary, fetch both postings lists and **intersect** them.

Because both lists are sorted, keep one pointer in each. Compare the two docIDs: if they are equal, output it and advance both; otherwise advance the pointer at the smaller docID, since that document cannot be in the other list.

blocks.title: Intersecting two postings lists with two pointers

scenes.caption: Two sorted postings lists. One pointer starts at the head of each. The answer list is empty.
Compare 2 with 5: 2 is smaller, so no document below 5 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 5 with 5: equal, so 5 goes into the answer and both pointers advance.
Compare 9 with 21: 9 is smaller, so no document below 21 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 14 with 21: 14 is smaller, so no document below 21 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 21 with 21: equal, so 21 goes into the answer and both pointers advance.
Compare 30 with 40: 30 is smaller, so no document below 40 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 38 with 40: 38 is smaller, so no document below 40 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 47 with 40: 40 is smaller, so advance p2.
Compare 47 with 47: equal, so 47 goes into the answer and both pointers advance. p2 has run off its list, so we stop: 9 comparisons in total, at most len(p1) + len(p2) = 12.

blocks.caption: Each comparison advances at least one pointer, so the merge does at most x + y steps.

blocks.md:
This only works because every postings list uses the same global order. OR (union) and AND NOT are merges in the same style.

For an AND of many terms, order matters. The standard heuristic is to process terms in **increasing df**: start with the two shortest lists, and every intermediate result is then no longer than the shortest list. The dictionary already holds df, so the engine can plan the order before reading any postings from disk.

blocks.prompt: A query is `kernel AND server AND crash` with df 200, 8 and 4. In what order should the lists be intersected?
blocks.reveal: Start with **crash (4) and server (8)**: their intersection has at most 4 documents (here 3: 5, 21, 47). Then check those few candidates against kernel's 200 postings. Starting with kernel AND server would first walk up to 208 entries to build an intermediate result that can still be no larger than 8.

blocks.md: When one list is much shorter than the other, even $O(x+y)$ wastes time walking the long list. **Skip pointers** add shortcuts at index time: some postings also store the position of a posting further ahead. If the skip target is still no larger than the docID we are looking for, we jump. A simple heuristic that works well in practice: for a list of length $P$, use $\sqrt{P}$ evenly spaced skips.

blocks.title: Skip pointers on a 16-entry postings list

scenes.caption: A 16-entry list uses skip spacing sqrt(16) = 4: every 4th entry also stores where to jump (2 to 15, 15 to 34, 34 to 58). 58 has no entry 4 ahead, so only 3 skips exist.
Without skips, intersecting with the one-entry list [47] walks p1 through 2, 4, 7, ..., 40 before reaching 47: 11 entries visited.
With skips: p1 is at 2 and 2 < 47. Its skip target 15 is still at most 47, so jump to 15 instead of stepping through 4, 7, 11.
15 has a skip to 34, and 34 is at most 47: jump again. 34 skips to 58, which is past 47, so that skip is not taken.
Step normally from 34 to 40 to 47: match. p1 landed on 5 entries (2, 15, 34, 40, 47) instead of 11, at the cost of storing and checking skip pointers.

blocks.md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.
Intersection is a linear merge over sorted lists. Make it cheap by starting from the rarest term, and make long lists skippable.

blocks.question: You intersect a 10-entry list with a 1,000,000-entry list using the plain two-pointer merge. Roughly how many steps can it take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because the result has at most 10 documents
About 20, because each short entry costs two comparisons
About 1,000,000, because the pointer may have to walk the long list nearly to its end
About log2(1,000,000) = 20 per entry, because the lists are sorted
blocks.explain: The plain merge advances one step at a time, so in the worst case it walks the whole long list: O(x + y). Doing about 20 steps per short entry is what you get only if you add skips or binary search into the long list, which the plain merge does not do.

blocks.question: Why does the engine keep df in the in-memory dictionary even for a pure Boolean search engine?
options: Boolean retrieval multiplies scores by df
It lets the planner order terms by list length before reading any postings
The merge algorithm needs df to know when to stop
It is needed to decompress postings
blocks.explain: Knowing each list's length up front lets the query optimizer intersect the shortest lists first. The merge itself stops when either pointer runs off its list, so it never needs df.

lessons.title: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity

blocks.md:
Boolean queries return sets. Most users type a **free text query** (a few words, no operators) and expect the best documents first. So we score each document.

Start with the **bag of words** view: a document is just the counts of its terms, ignoring order. *Mary is quicker than John* and *John is quicker than Mary* are the same bag. The count of term $t$ in document $d$ is its **term frequency** $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$.

The simplest score is the **overlap score**: add up, over the query terms, how many times each occurs in the document. Run it on our six documents for the query `the cache miss`. The user clearly cares about cache misses, and only d5 says *cache miss*.

blocks.prompt: With the overlap score (sum of tf over the, cache, miss), which document ranks first?
blocks.reveal: **d1**, with 5: three copies of *the* and two of *cache*. d5 scores 3 and ties with d2, d4 and d6. Raw counts treat every term as equally important, so the most common word in English does most of the scoring.

blocks.md: We need to discount terms that appear everywhere. One option is collection frequency, but document frequency works better for telling documents apart. In the Reuters collection, *try* and *insurance* occur about equally often in total (10,422 and 10,440 times), yet *try* is spread over 8,760 documents and *insurance* over only 3,997. A query on *insurance* should reward its documents more. The **inverse document frequency** of a term, for a collection of $N$ documents, is:

blocks.caption: A term in every document gets log(1) = 0. The rarer the term, the higher its idf.

scenes.caption: A term in one document out of a million gets idf 6. Every factor of 10 more documents costs exactly 1 point (log base 10).

blocks.md: The idea is older than the formula. In 1972 Karen Sparck Jones argued that matches on rare, specific terms should count for more than matches on frequent ones, and weighted a term occurring in $n$ of $N$ documents by $f(N) - f(n) + 1$ with $f(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$. In Sparck Jones's 200-document Cranfield example a term in 90 documents got weight 2 and a term in 3 documents got weight 7.
**TF-IDF** combines the two signals: the weight of term $t$ in document $d$ is its count times its rarity. A document's score for a query is the sum of the weights of the query terms:

blocks.title: Query the cache miss: raw counts vs TF-IDF

scenes.caption: Overlap score: total occurrences of query terms. d1 wins with 5, mostly from three copies of the and two of cache. d5, the only doc about a cache miss, ties with four others at 3.
TF-IDF with log10 idf: the gets idf 0, cache 0.176, miss 0.477. d5 now ranks first (0.653), then d6 (0.477) and d1 (0.352).

blocks.md: Twenty occurrences are unlikely to be twenty times as significant as one. A common fix is **sublinear tf scaling**: use $\mathrm{wf}_{t,d} = 1 + \log \mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$ when $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d} > 0$ (and 0 otherwise) in place of raw tf.

blocks.title: Raw tf versus sublinear tf weights

x.label: occurrences of the term in the doc (tf)

scenes.caption: Raw tf is linear: the 10th occurrence counts as much as the 1st.
Sublinear scaling 1 + log10(tf): one occurrence gives 1, ten give 2, twenty give 2.3. Repetition still helps, but with fast diminishing returns.
Lucene's classic TF-IDF used sqrt(tf): ten occurrences give 3.16. All three agree at tf = 1; they differ in how much repetition is rewarded.

blocks.md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

blocks.question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
blocks.explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

blocks.question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
blocks.explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

lessons.title: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity

blocks.md:
Treat each document as a vector with one dimension per dictionary term (17 here, hundreds of thousands in practice) and its tf-idf weights as coordinates. A query is just a very short document, so it becomes a vector too. Ranking becomes: which document vectors point in nearly the same direction as the query?

Why direction and not raw overlap? Two documents with the same mix of terms can have very different raw weights just because one is longer. The standard fix is the **cosine similarity**: the dot product of the two vectors divided by the product of their Euclidean lengths.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{score}(q,d) = \frac{\vec V(q) \cdot \vec V(d)}{|\vec V(q)|\,|\vec V(d)|} = \frac{\sum_t w_{t,q}\, w_{t,d}}{\sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,q}^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,d}^2}}
blocks.caption: Dividing by the lengths turns both vectors into unit vectors, so the score is the cosine of the angle between them, between 0 and 1 for non-negative weights.

blocks.title: TF-IDF weights before and after length normalization

scenes.caption: Raw tf-idf weights (tf x log10(N/df)) for 6 of the 17 terms. The column for the is all zero because it is in every document. d1 has cache weight 0.35 because cache occurs twice.
Divide each row by its document's full vector length (over all 17 terms): d1 1.472, d2 0.853, d5 1.087. d1's cache weight drops to 0.24, close to d2's 0.21.

After normalization every row is a unit vector, so a document cannot win just by having more or heavier terms. d5 has the largest weight on miss (0.44), the rarest query term, plus a weight on cache, so it will score highest.

blocks.md: For the query `the cache miss` we use idf as each query term's weight: $(0, 0.176, 0.477)$ for (the, cache, miss). Its length is 0.509, so the unit query vector is $(0, 0.346, 0.938)$. The query leans heavily toward *miss*, the rarest of its terms.

blocks.prompt: With plain TF-IDF sums, d1 scored 0.352 and d2 scored 0.176: d1 was twice as good. What happens to that gap under cosine scoring?
blocks.reveal: It nearly closes: **d1 0.083 vs d2 0.071**. d1 has four other non-zero terms (keeps, keys and in with idf 0.778 each, plus hot with 0.477), so its vector length is 1.472 against d2's 0.853. Its two copies of *cache* are a smaller share of a longer vector.

blocks.title: Cosine scores for the query the cache miss

scenes.caption: Full cosine: dot product divided by the document length and the query length 0.509. d5 0.468, d6 0.307, d1 0.083. The rare term miss decides most of the ranking.

blocks.md: Computing a dot product against every document would be far too slow. Instead, walk the postings of the query terms only. **Term-at-a-time** scoring keeps one **accumulator** per candidate document and adds each term's contribution as its postings are read. Postings store the integer tf, not a float weight; idf is derived from df (or $N/\mathrm{df}$ stored at the head of the list) at query time. A heap then extracts the top $K$. The alternative, **document-at-a-time**, walks all query lists together and finishes one document before moving on.

blocks.title: Term-at-a-time scoring with accumulators
blocks.code:
import math
N = 6
index = {"cache": [(1, 2), (2, 1), (4, 1), (5, 1)],
         "miss":  [(5, 1), (6, 1)]}
length = {1: 1.472, 2: 0.853, 4: 1.212, 5: 1.087, 6: 1.457}
scores = {}                      # accumulators
for term in ["cache", "miss"]:   # "the" has idf 0: skip it
    postings = index[term]
    idf = math.log10(N / len(postings))
    for doc, tf in postings:
        # query weight idf times doc weight tf*idf
        scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0) + idf * tf * idf
for doc in scores:
    scores[doc] /= length[doc]
top = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:3]
print([(d, round(s, 3)) for d, s in top])

scenes.caption: Postings store (docID, tf). Document vector lengths are precomputed at index time, over all terms of each document.
First query term cache: df 4, so idf = log10(6/4) = 0.176.
Walk cache's postings, adding each document's contribution to its accumulator. d1 has tf 2, so it gets twice as much.
Second term miss: idf 0.477. Only d5 and d6 are touched; d5's accumulator grows to 0.259.
Divide by document length. The query's length is the same for every document, so skipping it does not change the ranking.
Keep the top K (here 3). Large engines use a heap rather than a full sort.

blocks.md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

Cosine ranking does not require a document to contain all query terms. d6 never mentions *cache* yet ranks second, above d1 which has *cache* twice, because *miss* carries most of the query's weight. If you need every term, combine scoring with a Boolean AND filter.

The textbook SMART notation names a scheme as ddd.qqq: tf, df and normalization choices for documents, then for queries. A standard one is lnc.ltc: log tf, no idf and cosine normalization for documents; log tf, idf and cosine normalization for queries.

blocks.question: Using raw tf weights, you append a document to itself (every tf doubles, nothing else changes, and the document collection statistics stay the same). What happens to its cosine score for any query?
options: It doubles
It stays exactly the same
It increases by a factor of sqrt(2)
It drops, because the document is now longer
blocks.explain: With raw tf, every weight doubles, so the vector is scaled by 2. Scaling a vector does not change its direction, and cosine depends only on direction, so the score is unchanged. A plain TF-IDF sum would double, which is exactly the length bias cosine removes.

blocks.question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
blocks.explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

lessons.title: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene

blocks.md:
Postings dominate index size. The Reuters-RCV1 collection used in the textbook has 800,000 documents and 100,000,000 postings (docIDs only). A docID needs $\log_2 800{,}000 \approx 20$ bits, so the uncompressed postings take $10^8 \times 20 / 8 = 250$ MB.

The trick is that postings are sorted, so we can store **gaps** between consecutive docIDs. A frequent term appears in many nearby documents, so its gaps are small numbers that need far fewer bits.

blocks.title: Gap encoding plus variable byte codes

scenes.caption: A postings list of 5 docIDs. Stored as fixed 32-bit integers it takes 20 bytes.
Store the first docID, then only the gap to the previous one. Gaps are small when a term is frequent, because its documents are close together.
Variable byte: 7 payload bits per byte, with the high bit set on the last byte of each number. Gaps below 128 take 1 byte; 19869 needs 3. Total 7 bytes instead of 20.

blocks.md:
**Variable byte (VB)** encoding writes each gap in as few whole bytes as possible: 7 payload bits per byte, with the first bit as a continuation flag set on the last byte of a number. The textbook reports that VB shrinks the Reuters-RCV1 postings to 116 MB, more than a 50% saving. Byte-aligned codes decode fast; bit-level codes such as gamma codes compress further at the cost of more bit manipulation.

Lucene's 9.9 postings format goes a step further: docIDs and frequencies are delta-encoded and packed into blocks of 128 integers that share one bit width, with leftover entries written as variable-length ints, and with skip data per block.

blocks.prompt: Which postings list compresses better with gap encoding: the one for *the*, or the one for a term that appears in two documents far apart?
blocks.reveal: **the**. It occurs in almost every document, so nearly all its gaps are 1 and each fits in a single byte. A rare term's gaps are about as large as the docIDs themselves, so gap encoding saves almost nothing on it, though such lists are short anyway.

blocks.md:
Compression makes in-place updates awkward: a postings list is a contiguous, compressed run, and inserting into it means rewriting it. The textbook design for a changing collection keeps a large **main index** plus a small in-memory **auxiliary index** for new documents, searches both and merges results, records deletions in an invalidation bit vector, and merges the auxiliary index into the main one when it grows too large.

Lucene generalizes this into **segments**. Each segment is a complete, independent inverted index. New documents create new segments, existing segments are merged, and a search runs over all of them.

blocks.title: Where a Lucene segment keeps the inverted index

scenes.caption: The dictionary lives in .tim (term dictionary); .tip is a small index into it so a term lookup does not scan the whole file.
The term entry points into .doc: docIDs and frequencies, in the Lucene 9.9 format packed in blocks of 128 with skip data. Positions sit in .pos, read only for queries that need them.
Simplified: an index is many segments, each a complete inverted index. New documents go into new segments; background merges combine segments into larger ones.

blocks.md: Lucene shipped TF-IDF as its default ranking for years. Its `ClassicSimilarity` uses $\mathrm{tf} = \sqrt{\mathrm{freq}}$, $\mathrm{idf} = 1 + \ln\frac{\mathrm{docCount}+1}{\mathrm{docFreq}+1}$ and a length norm of $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{numTerms}}$. The +1 terms keep idf positive and finite even for a term in every document. Lucene 6.0 switched the default to BM25 ([LUCENE-6789](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/LUCENE-6789)); `ClassicSimilarity` remains available.

blocks.title: idf in the six-doc corpus: log10 vs Lucene classic

scenes.caption: Textbook idf log10(N/df): the term in every document gets exactly 0.
Lucene classic idf 1 + ln((N+1)/(df+1)): the gets 1.000, never 0, and the ratio between rare and common terms shrinks (keys/cache 1.69 vs 4.42).

blocks.md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

blocks.question: Using variable byte encoding (7 payload bits per byte), how many bytes does the gap 300 take?
options: 1 byte
2 bytes
3 bytes
4 bytes
blocks.explain: One byte holds values up to 127; two bytes hold 14 payload bits, values up to 16,383. 300 = 2 x 128 + 44, so it is written as the bytes 2 and 44, with the continuation bit set on the second byte.

blocks.question: Why does Lucene add documents by writing new segments instead of inserting postings into existing lists?
options: Segments are needed to compute idf
Postings are compressed contiguous runs, so in-place insertion would mean rewriting them; append-only segments plus background merges avoid that
Each segment can only hold one field
Lucene cannot store more than 128 documents per segment
blocks.explain: Compressed, gap-encoded postings cannot absorb an insert cheaply. Writing a fresh small segment is fast, and merges later rewrite several segments into one larger, well-compressed segment. This is the same main plus auxiliary idea from the textbook, generalized to many segments. The 128 is the packed block size, not a segment limit.
